questions.questionText: Which statement describes the particles in a liquid?
options: They are close together, in an irregular arrangement, and slide past each other.
They are far apart, in a regular pattern, and vibrate.
They are far apart and move randomly at high speed.
They are close together, in a fixed regular pattern, and vibrate.
questions.correctAnswer: They are close together, in an irregular arrangement, and slide past each other.
questions.explanation: Liquid particles are close together but irregularly arranged and can move around each other, so liquids flow but have a fixed volume.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to describe liquid particle arrangement and motion. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 1; proposed alignment P2.1.2.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Which property is true for a gas but NOT for a liquid?
questions.correctAnswer: It has no fixed volume.
questions.explanation: Both liquids and gases have no fixed shape, but only a gas has no fixed volume — it fills its container.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to distinguish gas and liquid volume properties. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 2; proposed alignment P2.1.1.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Smoke particles in air are seen through a microscope moving in a random, jerky way. What causes this motion?
options: Collisions between the smoke particles themselves
The smoke particles being heated by the microscope light
Collisions of fast-moving, much smaller air molecules with the smoke particles
questions.correctAnswer: Collisions of fast-moving, much smaller air molecules with the smoke particles
questions.explanation: Brownian motion: light, fast-moving air molecules hit the larger smoke particles unevenly from all sides, pushing them randomly.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain Brownian motion using molecular collisions. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 3; proposed alignment P2.1.2.5; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: A sealed container of gas is heated. Its volume stays the same. Why does the pressure increase?
options: The particles stop colliding with each other.
The particles move faster, hitting the walls more often and with greater force.
questions.correctAnswer: The particles move faster, hitting the walls more often and with greater force.
questions.explanation: Higher temperature means higher average kinetic energy, so collisions with the walls are more frequent and each has a larger change of momentum.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain gas pressure increase at constant volume. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 6; proposed alignment P2.1.3.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: How do gas particles exert a pressure on the walls of their container?
options: Their change of momentum when they hit the walls produces a force on the walls.
They stick to the walls and push outwards.
Their weight pushes down on the base of the container only.
They are attracted to the particles of the wall.
questions.correctAnswer: Their change of momentum when they hit the walls produces a force on the walls.
questions.explanation: Each collision changes the particle's momentum, which needs a force; the total force per unit area of wall is the pressure.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain gas pressure using wall collisions. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 7; proposed alignment P2.1.2.6; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: The volume of a fixed mass of gas is doubled while its temperature stays constant. What happens to its pressure?
questions.correctAnswer: It halves.
questions.explanation: pV = constant, so if V doubles, p must halve. Particles hit each unit area of wall less often.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to predict pressure change at constant temperature. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 9; proposed alignment P2.1.3.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: A gas is cooled at constant volume. Which quantity decreases?
options: The average kinetic energy of the particles
questions.correctAnswer: The average kinetic energy of the particles
questions.explanation: Temperature is linked to the average kinetic energy of the particles; mass, size and number of particles do not change.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to relate temperature to average particle kinetic energy. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 10; proposed alignment P2.1.2.2; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: For typical materials at constant pressure, equal initial volumes of a solid, a liquid and a gas have the same temperature rise. What is the usual order of increasing expansion?
questions.correctAnswer: solid, liquid, gas
questions.explanation: Typically, solids expand least, liquids more and gases most. Particular substances and conditions can show exceptions.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to compare thermal expansion of states of matter. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 11; proposed alignment P2.2.1.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Why are small gaps left between sections of a concrete bridge?
options: To allow the sections to expand in hot weather without cracking
questions.correctAnswer: To allow the sections to expand in hot weather without cracking
questions.explanation: Concrete expands when heated; without gaps the expanding sections would push against each other and crack or buckle.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain expansion gaps in structures. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 12; proposed alignment P2.2.1.2; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Why does a metal rod expand when it is heated?
options: The particles vibrate with larger amplitude and move further apart on average.
questions.correctAnswer: The particles vibrate with larger amplitude and move further apart on average.
questions.explanation: Heating increases the kinetic energy of the particles, so they vibrate more and their average separation increases.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain expansion using mean particle separation. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 13; proposed alignment P2.1.2.4; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: An object is heated and its temperature rises without a change of state. What happens to the average kinetic energy of its particles?
questions.correctAnswer: Their average kinetic energy increases.
questions.explanation: A rise in temperature corresponds to an increase in the average kinetic energy of the particles.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to relate temperature to average particle kinetic energy. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 17; proposed alignment P2.1.2.2; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Ice at 0 °C is heated and melts. The temperature stays at 0 °C until all the ice has melted. Why?
options: The particles slow down as the ice melts.
Energy is being lost to the surroundings as fast as it is supplied.
The energy supplied increases particle potential energy by overcoming attractive forces, rather than increasing average kinetic energy.
questions.correctAnswer: The energy supplied increases particle potential energy by overcoming attractive forces, rather than increasing average kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: During a change of state the energy supplied increases the potential energy of the particles (separating them), not their kinetic energy, so temperature is constant.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain constant temperature during melting. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 18; proposed alignment P2.2.2.5; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Why does evaporation cause a liquid to cool down?
options: The most energetic particles escape, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles falls.
Air above the liquid takes in heat by conduction only.
The particles in the liquid get smaller.
The least energetic particles escape from the surface.
questions.correctAnswer: The most energetic particles escape, so the average kinetic energy of the remaining particles falls.
questions.explanation: More energetic particles are more likely to escape. Their loss reduces the average kinetic energy of the particles remaining in the liquid, causing cooling.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain evaporative cooling through particle energies. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 19; proposed alignment P2.2.2.3; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: At constant pressure, which statement correctly compares evaporation and boiling?
options: Evaporation happens throughout the liquid; boiling happens only at the surface.
Both happen only at a fixed temperature.
Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.
Boiling can happen at any temperature; evaporation happens only at 100 °C.
questions.correctAnswer: Evaporation happens only at the surface and at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature.
questions.explanation: Evaporation occurs at the surface over a range of temperatures. A pure liquid boils throughout its volume at its boiling point for the given pressure.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to distinguish boiling and evaporation. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 20; proposed alignment P2.2.2.6; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Why are metals good thermal conductors?
options: They are good absorbers of infrared radiation.
They contain free (delocalised) electrons that carry energy through the metal.
Their atoms are very far apart.
questions.correctAnswer: They contain free (delocalised) electrons that carry energy through the metal.
questions.explanation: In metals, free electrons move quickly through the lattice and transfer energy, in addition to atomic vibrations.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain thermal conduction using mobile electrons. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 21; proposed alignment P2.3.1.2; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: How is thermal energy conducted through a non-metal such as glass?
options: By free electrons moving through the glass
By the glass particles moving from the hot end to the cold end
By vibrating atoms passing energy to neighbouring atoms
questions.correctAnswer: By vibrating atoms passing energy to neighbouring atoms
questions.explanation: Energy is passed between neighbouring atoms through vibrations. Glass has no mobile conduction electrons comparable to those in metals; it is generally a poor thermal conductor.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain conduction through particle vibrations. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 22; proposed alignment P2.3.1.2; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Why can convection NOT happen in a solid?
options: Solids do not expand when heated.
The particles in a solid cannot move from place to place.
questions.correctAnswer: The particles in a solid cannot move from place to place.
questions.explanation: Convection needs the heated material itself to flow. Particles in a solid only vibrate about fixed positions.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to identify why convection requires a flowing medium. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 23; proposed alignment P2.3.2.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Why is a room heater usually placed near the floor?
options: Air near the heater expands, becomes less dense and rises, setting up a convection current.
Thermal energy is conducted through the air to the ceiling.
Cold air cannot be heated near the ceiling.
Hot air is denser and sinks to the floor.
questions.correctAnswer: Air near the heater expands, becomes less dense and rises, setting up a convection current.
questions.explanation: Warm air is less dense, so it rises; cooler, denser air moves in to replace it, circulating heat around the room.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain convection through density changes. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 24; proposed alignment P2.3.2.3; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Which method of thermal energy transfer can take place through a vacuum?
questions.correctAnswer: Thermal radiation
questions.explanation: Thermal radiation transfers energy electromagnetically and requires no material medium. It is mainly infrared at ordinary temperatures.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to identify radiation as energy transfer through vacuum. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 25; proposed alignment P2.3.3.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Four identical cans contain equal masses of water at the same initial temperature in the same cooler surroundings. Their surfaces differ. Which is expected to lose energy fastest by thermal radiation?
questions.correctAnswer: Dull black
questions.explanation: Dull black surfaces are the best emitters (and absorbers) of infrared radiation.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to compare thermal emission from different surfaces. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 26; proposed alignment P2.3.3.2; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: A kettle is designed to lose as little energy as possible by radiation. Which outer surface is best?
questions.correctAnswer: Shiny silver
questions.explanation: Shiny, light surfaces are poor emitters of infrared, so a shiny silver kettle loses energy by radiation most slowly.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to compare thermal emission from different surfaces. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 27; proposed alignment P2.3.3.2; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: If the average temperature of the Earth is constant over a long period, which energy balance must hold?
options: The Earth absorbs no radiation from the Sun.
The rate at which the Earth absorbs radiation equals the rate at which it emits radiation.
The Earth emits no radiation into space.
The atmosphere stops all infrared radiation.
questions.correctAnswer: The rate at which the Earth absorbs radiation equals the rate at which it emits radiation.
questions.explanation: A constant average temperature requires the average absorbed and emitted radiation powers to balance. A sustained imbalance changes the stored energy and temperature.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain temperature stability using radiation balance. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 29; proposed alignment P2.3.3.3; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: In a vacuum flask, what is the main purpose of the vacuum between the two walls?
options: To reduce energy transfer by radiation
To reduce energy transfer by conduction and convection
To increase energy transfer by convection
questions.correctAnswer: To reduce energy transfer by conduction and convection
questions.explanation: Conduction and convection need particles; the vacuum has none. The silvered walls are what reduce radiation.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain vacuum insulation against conduction and convection. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 30; proposed alignment P2.3.4.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Which pair of particle types can be found in atomic nuclei?
questions.correctAnswer: Protons and neutrons
questions.explanation: Nuclei contain protons and usually neutrons; hydrogen-1 is the common exception with a single proton and no neutron. Electrons occupy the region outside the nucleus.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to identify nuclear constituents. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 31; proposed alignment P5.1.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: A nuclide is written as ²³₁₁Na. How many protons and neutrons does its nucleus contain?
questions.correctAnswer: 11 protons, 12 neutrons
questions.explanation: Proton number Z = 11; nucleon number A = 23; neutrons = A − Z = 23 − 11 = 12.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to calculate proton and neutron numbers from nuclide notation. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 32; proposed alignment P5.1.3; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: What are isotopes of an element?
options: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
Atoms with different numbers of electrons only
Atoms with the same number of neutrons but different numbers of protons
Atoms with the same nucleon number but different proton numbers
questions.correctAnswer: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same proton number (same element) but different neutron numbers, so different nucleon numbers.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to distinguish isotopes using proton and neutron numbers. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 33; proposed alignment P5.1.5; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: What happens in nuclear fission?
options: A nucleus absorbs a gamma ray and becomes stable.
Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus.
An electron is emitted from the nucleus.
A large, unstable nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy.
questions.correctAnswer: A large, unstable nucleus splits into two smaller nuclei, releasing energy.
questions.explanation: In fission, a heavy nucleus (e.g. uranium-235, after absorbing a neutron) splits into two smaller nuclei plus neutrons, releasing energy.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to distinguish nuclear fission from fusion. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 36; proposed alignment P5.1.7; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: What happens in nuclear fusion?
options: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
A heavy nucleus splits into two lighter nuclei.
A neutron changes into a proton.
questions.correctAnswer: Two light nuclei join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy.
questions.explanation: Fusion joins light nuclei (e.g. hydrogen into helium). It is the energy source of stars.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to distinguish nuclear fusion from fission. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 37; proposed alignment P5.1.7; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Which of these is a source of background radiation?
questions.correctAnswer: Radon gas from rocks
questions.explanation: Radon gas, rocks and buildings, cosmic rays, food and medical sources contribute to background radiation. The others give non-ionising radiation.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to identify sources of ionising background radiation. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 38; proposed alignment P5.2.1.2; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: What is an alpha particle?
options: A helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons
questions.correctAnswer: A helium nucleus: 2 protons and 2 neutrons
questions.explanation: An alpha particle is ⁴₂He: two protons and two neutrons, with a charge of +2.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to identify alpha particle composition. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 40; proposed alignment P5.2.2.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: What is a beta-minus particle?
options: A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
An electron from the outer shell of the atom
questions.correctAnswer: A high-speed electron emitted from the nucleus
questions.explanation: A beta particle is a fast-moving electron produced in, and emitted from, the nucleus.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to identify beta-minus particles. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 41; proposed alignment P5.2.2.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: What is gamma radiation?
questions.correctAnswer: Electromagnetic radiation
questions.explanation: Gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves with no mass and no charge.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to identify gamma as electromagnetic radiation. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 42; proposed alignment P5.2.2.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Which type of radiation is the most strongly ionising?
questions.correctAnswer: Alpha
questions.explanation: Alpha particles are large and have a +2 charge, so they ionise strongly — which is also why their range is short.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to compare ionising effects of nuclear emissions. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 43; proposed alignment P5.2.2.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: A radiation passes through a sheet of paper but is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Which type is it?
questions.correctAnswer: Beta
questions.explanation: Alpha is stopped by paper; beta needs a few mm of aluminium; gamma is only reduced by thick lead or concrete.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to identify emissions using absorber evidence. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 44; proposed alignment P5.2.2.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Which type of radiation is the most penetrating?
questions.correctAnswer: Gamma
questions.explanation: Of alpha, beta and gamma radiation, gamma is the most penetrating. Thick lead or concrete attenuates gamma radiation; it is not stopped at a single definite range.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to compare penetration of nuclear emissions. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 45; proposed alignment P5.2.2.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Radium-226 (²²⁶₈₈Ra) decays by emitting an alpha particle. Which nuclide is produced?
questions.correctAnswer: ²²²₈₆Rn
questions.explanation: Alpha decay removes ⁴₂He: nucleon number 226 − 4 = 222, proton number 88 − 2 = 86 (radon).

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to determine daughter nuclides after alpha decay. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 48; proposed alignment P5.2.3.4; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Carbon-14 (¹⁴₆C) decays by beta-minus emission. Which nuclide is produced?
questions.correctAnswer: ¹⁴₇N
questions.explanation: In beta decay the nucleon number is unchanged (14) and the proton number increases by 1 (6 → 7, nitrogen).

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to determine daughter nuclides after beta-minus decay. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 49; proposed alignment P5.2.3.4; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: What happens inside the nucleus during beta-minus decay?
options: Two protons and two neutrons are emitted.
An electron is captured from the outer shell.
A proton changes into a neutron and an electron.
A neutron changes into a proton and an electron.
questions.correctAnswer: A neutron changes into a proton and an electron.
questions.explanation: A neutron changes into a proton and an electron; the electron is emitted. An electron antineutrino is also emitted, although it is outside the required 0654 description.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to describe nuclear change in beta-minus emission. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 50; proposed alignment P5.2.3.3; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: A nucleus emits a gamma ray. What happens to its proton number and nucleon number?
options: Proton number increases by 1; nucleon number is unchanged.
Proton number decreases by 2; nucleon number decreases by 4.
questions.correctAnswer: Both stay the same.
questions.explanation: Gamma emission releases nuclear energy as a photon. The numbers of protons and neutrons remain unchanged.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to determine nucleon and proton changes in gamma emission. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 51; proposed alignment P5.2.3.4; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Which statement about radioactive decay is correct?
options: It can be stopped by putting the source in a magnetic field.
Each nucleus decays at a predictable time.
It speeds up when the source is heated.
questions.correctAnswer: It is random and spontaneous.
questions.explanation: Decay is random (we cannot predict which nucleus decays next) and spontaneous (unaffected by temperature, pressure or chemical changes).

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain random and spontaneous radioactive decay. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 52; proposed alignment P5.2.3.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: What is meant by the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
options: Half the time taken for all the nuclei to decay
The time taken for half the nuclei in a sample to decay
The time taken for the mass of the sample to halve because of evaporation
The time taken for the count rate to fall to zero
questions.correctAnswer: The time taken for half the nuclei in a sample to decay
questions.explanation: Half-life is the time for half the initially undecayed nuclei to decay. The source count rate also halves over this interval when background is negligible or properly corrected.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to define radioactive half-life. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.

assessmentProfile.sourceReference: Uploaded source question 53; proposed alignment P5.2.4.1; https://www.cambridgeinternational.org/Images/664572-2025-2027-syllabus.pdf. Not a Cambridge exam item or endorsement.

questions.questionText: Why is an alpha source used in smoke detectors?
options: Alpha sources have very short half-lives.
Alpha radiation is very penetrating, so it reaches every room.
Alpha radiation strongly ionises the air; smoke reduces the ionisation current.
Alpha radiation is not affected by smoke.
questions.correctAnswer: Alpha radiation strongly ionises the air; smoke reduces the ionisation current.
questions.explanation: The sealed alpha source ionises air so a small current flows. Smoke reduces this current and triggers the alarm. Its short range limits external exposure in an intact detector; radioactive sources still require controlled handling.

taxonomies.evidenceStatement: A correct response supports the ability to explain alpha radiation use in smoke detectors. It does not identify every reasoning step or establish mastery alone.
